tagline.text: Antique's gem, where a white sandbar curves beneath green hills

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May (dry season, when the sea is calm)

children.text: A small island off Culasi on Panay's west coast, where grassy green hills meet a white sandbar, earning it the nickname "little Batanes." Stay a night at a resident-run homestay and quietly enjoy hilltop sunsets and coral seas.
Mararison Island is a small island about
2.5km
off the coast of Culasi in northern Antique province, also locally called "Malalison." It covers only about 0.55 square kilometers, and even its highest point, Tuyong-tuyong Hill, rises to a modest

. Still, the sight of grass-covered rolling hills flowing down toward the sea, curving into a white sandbar at their edge, is so striking that Filipino travelers compare it to the country's northernmost islands and call it "the little Batanes of the Visayas."

About 800 residents, including descendants of the Karay-a and Ati peoples, live on the island by fishing. The surrounding reef has more than 100 species of hard coral, so even simple snorkeling shows off vivid coral and tropical fish, and Nablak Island, an uninhabited island about
0.8km

to the west, can be reached on foot at low tide or by a short boat ride. The Kawit Sandbar on the island's east side changes length and shape with the tide, so the scene looks different in the morning and afternoon even on the same day.
The island began attracting attention after being featured in the media following Typhoon Haiyan in

, and while Antique province has developed it into a signature destination, it chose a community-based tourism model where residents run the guiding and homestays themselves. As a result, simple guesthouses and a fishing-village atmosphere remain in place of large resorts or busy shopping streets. Behind the island, a mountain range including Mount Madja-as, Panay's highest peak (about
), stands like a screen, letting you frame sea and mountains in a single view.

It suits travelers who value quiet and natural scenery over amenities, those weary of Boracay's crowds, and photo-loving couples or friend trips. If you can accept that electricity, water, and communication aren't as abundant as in the city, it makes for an unforgettable night.
Follow a grassy path from the village for about
20–30 minutes
to reach a ridge overlooking the whole island, the sandbar, and Nablak Island. This is where Mararison's signature photos come from.
A snow-white sandbar stretching out to the east of the island, beautiful where waves from either side meet. Go when the tide is out to walk all the way to the end of the sandbar.
Swim just a few dozen meters out from the beach and the coral colonies begin. Gear can be rented on the island for about
for
3–4 hours
A small uninhabited island to the west, crossed on foot at low tide or by bangka (about
round trip) at high tide. You can observe small marine life among the rocks and tide pools.

Once the day-trippers have all left, the island takes on an entirely different mood. Experience island life up close, from the sunset over the hills to a sky full of stars and fishermen heading out at dawn.
Buy fish, squid, or shellfish at the Culasi market, or ask an island resident, and for a small cooking fee they'll grill it or prepare it as kilawin (vinegar-cured ceviche).

children.text: Watch the sunrise and the Panay mountain range from the hill or beach

For a day trip, arrive in Culasi early in the morning, enjoy the sandbar, the hill, and snorkeling in turn, and head back on a late-afternoon boat. Confirm the last boat time with the tourism office in advance.
Fly from Manila to Caticlan Airport (MPH) or Kalibo International Airport (KLO), about
1 hour
, then travel overland to Culasi. Caticlan is closer, while Kalibo often has cheaper fares.
Using Iloilo International Airport (ILO), it's about
4–5 hours
overland to Culasi via San Jose, the capital of Antique.
From Kalibo terminal, take a bus or van bound for San Jose, Antique, and get off in Culasi town. It takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
, for around
Buses and vans bound for southern Antique also run near Caticlan (the Boracay jetty), taking about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
to Culasi. It's a good stop after a Boracay trip.
Register as a visitor at the tourism office near Culasi town hall, pay the environmental and registration fee (about
per person), and you'll be assigned a bangka. Fees and rules can change, so check the latest notices.
The bangka takes about
15–20 minutes
to the island, costing about
round trip per boat for up to 5 people. For larger groups, it's charged per person.
There are no cars on the island, and everywhere is reached on foot. It's about
10 minutes
from the village to the sandbar, and about
20–30 minutes
to the viewpoint hill. In Culasi town, it's a short tricycle ride from town to the wharf.
Because Mararison Island sits on Panay's west coast, the sea stays relatively calm even during the northeast monsoon of
November–February
, and
March–May
, the peak of the dry season, brings the clearest water, ideal for snorkeling and sandbar photos. Midday temperatures during this period reach
, though, and the hills have almost no shade, so plan your climb for morning or dusk.
June–October

is when the southwest monsoon hits the west coast head-on, bringing high waves, and bangka service stops when a typhoon or strong wind advisory is issued. On clear days during this period, though, the hills turn their deepest green and visitors are fewer. The hillside grass can dry to yellow by the end of the dry season, so if green-hill photos are your goal, right after the wet season or
November–January
is best.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Lodging on the island is mostly homestays converted from residents' houses, at about

per person, per night. Fan rooms with a shared bathroom are standard, and some houses only have electricity at night or require you to conserve water. You can also pitch a tent on the beach or rent a cottage; if you want more amenities, it's better to stay at a pension in Culasi town or a resort in nearby Tibiao and visit the island as a day trip.

The island has almost no proper restaurants, so it's common to ask your homestay host to cook for you, or to buy fish, squid, shellfish, rice, and water at Culasi's public market and have it prepared there. Freshly caught grilled fish, vinegar-cured kilawin, and seafood simmered in coconut milk are the signature dishes. There are small sari-sari stores selling snacks and drinks, but the selection is limited, so bring anything you'll need in advance.
There's no ATM on the island. Bring cash for the bangka, homestay, guide, and meals, and carry plenty of small bills.
Check the tide chart in advance. The sandbar is longest and you can walk to Nablak Island at low tide.
The hill trek is short but has an incline and no shade. Bring a hat, water, and non-slip sandals or sneakers.
The viewpoint ridge has no railing. Don't get too close to the edge while taking photos.
Bring a power bank and a flashlight. Electricity and cell signal on the island can be unreliable.
Day-trippers flock here on weekends and holidays. For a quiet island, stay overnight on a weekday.
To protect the reef, use reef-safe sunscreen, and take your trash back out with you.

When waves are high or a strong wind advisory is issued, bangka service stops and you can be stranded on the island. Build a spare day into your itinerary during the wet season, and check with the Culasi tourism office and weather information before you set out.
Currents pick up with the tide at the end of the sandbar and in the channel between the islands. Don't wade out into deep water as the tide comes in.
Picking or taking plants like the hillside pitcher plants, or coral, is prohibited.
The island has no hospital. Bring basic medicine and antiseptic, and wash any coral scrapes immediately.
When passing through residents' homes and the village, don't take photos without permission, and don't make loud noise late at night.
Wear a life jacket when riding the bangka, and keep your phone and wallet in a waterproof bag.

from Culasi by car, a river town known for river kayaking, tiered waterfalls, and hot cauldron baths.
